overview: This card follows the modern Republic of Azerbaijan, including mainland territory and the separate Nakhchivan component shown by the atlas. Independence returned in 1991, before this record begins in 1994. The older map outlines remain unchanged through 2020 despite war and displacement; a later outline replaces them. These shapes cannot show who controlled every place at a particular moment. Earlier khanates, the Soviet republic and the separate 1914 to 1938 Azerbaijan record have their own histories.

periods.title: Post-Soviet institutions
periods.summary: The 1995 constitution established the framework for the independent republic during a period of strong presidential government.

periods.title: Succession and energy connections
periods.summary: Ilham Aliyev succeeded his father after the 2003 presidential election. The Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline opened a new oil-export route in 2006.

periods.title: Renewed war and humanitarian needs
periods.summary: The 2020 fighting damaged homes and public services, leaving families displaced and communities facing mines and missing relatives.

periods.title: Displacement and restricted political competition
periods.summary: The September 2023 crisis drove over 100,000 ethnic Armenians to Armenia. Observers criticized the lack of genuine alternatives in the 2024 presidential election.

periods.title: An ongoing peace process
periods.summary: Leaders signed a joint declaration in August 2025. An August 2026 trilateral statement reported border stability and continuing work to normalize relations.

items.text: Azerbaijan regained independence as the Soviet Union broke up in 1991. The United States recognized it that December and established diplomatic relations in February 1992. This was a new international setting for a republic whose earlier independence had ended with the Red Army’s arrival in 1920. The atlas’s 1994 start is therefore a display boundary, not the country’s birthday.

Voters adopted a constitution on 12 November 1995. Its text describes a secular, unitary republic and divides state power among legislative, executive and judicial institutions. It also sets out rights to education and use of a native language. These are constitutional commitments; how government worked in practice also requires evidence about elections and public services.

In the 2003 election, Heydar Aliyev withdrew in favor of his son Ilham, who was declared the winner. International observers found serious shortcomings, including intimidation and unequal campaign conditions. The succession preserved a powerful presidency. Two decades later, OSCE observers described the February 2024 election as efficiently prepared but lacking genuine pluralism, with critical voices suppressed.

Nagorno-Karabakh was internationally recognized as part of Azerbaijan, while Armenian-backed forces controlled it after the war ending in 1994. Azerbaijan regained parts of the region and surrounding territory in the 2020 war. A further Azerbaijani offensive in September 2023 defeated the remaining Armenian forces there. These different military situations should not be read from one unchanged atlas outline.

The human consequences crossed borders. UNHCR and partners recorded that more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians fled Nagorno-Karabakh to Armenia during the last week of September 2023. Families urgently needed housing, healthcare and schooling. This refugee movement is central to the period’s history, alongside the earlier displacement of Azerbaijanis, rather than a small footnote to changes on a map.

The December 2020 ICRC report describes damaged homes, schools and hospitals across the conflict region. Its response included new showers and latrines for 66 families living in shelters. A working toilet and a place to wash could matter immediately to people forced from home. These are regional aid figures, not a claim that every family in Azerbaijan lacked sanitation.

In June 2006, the tanker British Hawthorn left Ceyhan in Turkey with the first cargo delivered by the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline. The route carried Caspian oil from Azerbaijan through Georgia to the Mediterranean. Thousands of workers from the three countries helped build this connection. A ship leaving one port could mark the result of years of work far inland.

Modern Baku also had to look after its older buildings. UNESCO removed its walled city, Shirvanshah’s Palace and Maiden Tower from the Danger List in 2009 after preservation improved. Earthquake damage and poorly controlled development had threatened the historic area. Repairing and protecting inherited buildings is an achievement of the modern city, even though the monuments themselves are much older.

Dolma can be a tiny edible parcel: a filling of ingredients such as meat, onion, rice and spices wrapped in leaves or tucked into vegetables. UNESCO’s 2017 description emphasizes sharing within families and communities, with recipes varying between them. Children can learn alongside parents, while vocational schools teach the craft too. There is more than one way to make dinner fit inside its own wrapper.

Carpet weaving joins skilled hands across generations. UNESCO describes girls learning from mothers and grandmothers in weaving families, often during winter. Some carpets use knotted pile; others have a flatter woven surface. Finishing one can be an occasion for a solemn celebration when it is cut from the loom. A floor covering may contain a great many patient afternoons.

Tea makes room for conversation. A joint UNESCO listing for Azerbaijan and Türkiye describes freshly brewed tea served in pear-shaped cups, with accompaniments such as sweets, lemon or jam. Hospitality is part of the practice: the cup helps mark a welcome and sustain social ties. This is shared regional heritage, with room for different household habits.

Preschool access grew, although it remained far from universal. UNICEF reported that enrollment rose from 14 percent in 2015 to 35 percent in 2024, following national investment in early learning. For families, such programs create places where young children can play, learn and prepare for school. The figures describe those years, not a promise that every child already has a place.

Support for a small child can begin at home. UNICEF describes a home-visiting model in which health workers help families with vaccination, developmental checks and early concerns. Such visits connect child health with the people doing everyday care. They can help a parent notice a difficulty sooner instead of waiting until a child reaches school.

The constitution’s Article 42 begins: “Hər bir vətəndaşın təhsil almaq hüququ vardır.” Its official English version says: “Every citizen has the right to education.” This is Azerbaijani in its modern Latin alphabet, including the letter ə. The sample comes from the government’s current consolidated text of the 1995 constitution, shown here in modern type, rather than a photograph of its original publication.

A 2024 WHO and European Observatory review describes mandatory health insurance covering residents for a range of emergency, primary and hospital services. Important gaps remained: most outpatient medicines and dental care were outside the package. Rural shortages of staff and facilities also limited access. Having a right to treatment and finding nearby, affordable treatment are related but different challenges.

In Shamakhi, three mobile clinics brought equipped medical vehicles and trained workers to rural communities in a WHO-supported project reported in 2021. The team included family doctors and pediatricians, with drivers trained for the outreach work. Sometimes getting care closer to home meant putting part of the doctor’s office on wheels.

sections.title: Water at home and a continuing country

items.text: For some families, a water project changed an everyday chore. A World Bank account from Siyazan describes a resident who previously carried buckets and later could use water from taps for washing and cleaning. Across eight selected districts, project results through 2019 recorded over 46,000 household connections to new piped water. These improvements were substantial, but the eight districts were not the entire country.

The same project connected 43,000 households to new sewer networks and invested in wastewater treatment. Water arriving at a tap is only half the job: used water also needs somewhere safe to go. These figures document infrastructure, not a count of particular toilet designs in every home. Sanitation improvements often happen underground, where visitors never see the work.

Diplomacy remained a process. Armenia and Azerbaijan signed a joint declaration at the August 2025 Washington summit, while their foreign ministers initialed a draft interstate agreement. A joint statement with the United States dated 10 August 2026 reported border stability and continuing normalization and boundary work. Signing a declaration, initialing a draft and implementing a lasting settlement are different steps.

ending.text: Azerbaijan continues as a state; the atlas gives this record no historical end date. Its modern polygon’s 2100 endpoint is a rendering horizon, not a prediction. The August 2026 trilateral statement described continuing work on relations and borders with Armenia. That dated account cannot guarantee future peace or turn the map into a live record of control. Communities, family traditions and public services continue to change within this political history.
